# Abstract:

Give a title to your project. In an abstract of 200 words or less,
describe what is the main question you aim to answer, and a brief
summary of your current results.

- TITLE: Investigating Possible Income-Dependence in Disease and Illness
- This is an observational study using two publicly available data sets
  to analyze correlation between income and various health statuses. We
  investigate using median household income by county in the United
  States data from the US Census Bureau and population health data by
  county in the United States by the CDC. Using the computational tool
  R, we combine the data sets and isolate comparisons for analysis with
  the following findings. Health status seems to be negatively
  correlated with income. That is, the data shows counties with higher
  median household incomes had less adverse health statuses across
  various types of health status and various income brackets. The report
  will provide two analyses delving into income's relation to diabetes and depression and provide visual
  maps which depict the correlation we found.

# Intro

What is the central question that motivates your analysis? Who may this
analysis benefit? Are you trying to train a model, test a hypothesis,
classify objects apart? Why? This has to be written with proper grammar
and syntax: sentences, paragraphs, and a narrative structure.

- The question we are seeking to answer is whether income (whether it be
  higher or lower) has an effect on disease prevalence. Will median
  household income show a correlation to disease proclivity? If an increase
  in income does prove to have a negative affect on disease prevalence,
  the information we find could possibly help find a solution to this
  issue for interested parties. This can manifest in providing
  easier access to necessary healthcare for lower-income individuals, or helping
  better conditions to prevent the diseases from occurring.
  Alternatively, certain companies and investors may benefit
  from such a relationship being found by providing insight into the
  likelihood of certain investments succeeding in a population due to
  their proximity to disease and their relative wealth.

To realize these possible benefits, we are creating correlation maps
using publicly available data on the incomes of household in the US and
comparing these numbers to CDC estimates from 2025 for health status.

# Executive Summary

- Provide, in a series of 3-5 bullet points, what are the core
  conclusions and findings of your analysis so far.

  1.  Negative correlation exists between increasing income and disease rate.
      We are projecting our observations of diabetes and depression prevalence 
      in correlation to income for this conclusion, but further analysis of 
      different health statuses is possible.
  2.  Through a regression model for diabetes, we see that Median Household
      Income is statistically significant, and that it accurately
      explains \~45% of the variation in diabetes prevalence.
  3.  Through linear and quadratic regression we can see that the model
      for diabetes is quadratic, with diabetes prevalence decreasing
      at lower incomes, but slowly leveling out. At some point in the higher incomes, the line
      even upturns very little. Minimum diabetes prevalence is around
      median income of \$108k.
  4.  A graph for depression prevalence in correlation to income shows a
      similar relationship. It is also a quadratic line representing a negative 
      relationship with a decreasing prevalence as income increases. 
      However, the most notable difference is the depression graph doesn't show 
      any upturn at any moment, suggesting that prevalence continually 
      decreases. Depression rates drop continually as income increases.

# Data

What is the data available for performing the analysis? Where did you
retrieve these data from? What are the variables and number of
observations available? What steps where performed to clean the data? If
the data is obtained via randomized simulations, clarify the data
generating procedure

- US Census Bureau's data set for "Median Household Income in the Past
  12 Months in 2023" \@
  <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2023.B19013> This data set
  includes 3222 observations across 5 variables representing the
  geographic ID of a county, the name of the county, the median income,
  the margin of error, and the FIPS codes of the households surveyed. We
  used this data set to show the different median household income in
  each US county. To clean the data set, we first renamed the columns
  for clarity. Then, we changed the GeoId into a compatible FIPS code.

- CDC data set for "Local Data for Better Health, County Data in 2025"
  \@
  <https://data.cdc.gov/500-Cities-Places/PLACES-Local-Data-for-Better-Health-County-Data-20/swc5-untb/about_data>
  This data set includes 229298 observations across 22 variables
  representing both location names (geographic ID, state name, etc) and
  the estimates for measures (health outcomes, health status,
  disability, etc) within those locations. Using this data set, we can
  find the percentage amounts of disease from each county. To clean this
  code, all we did was convert the FIPS code into a numeric.

  With the FIPS code from each data set, we were able to merge the data
  sets and compare them directly. To clean this new data set, we changes
  the Median Household Income and the Total Population columns into
  numerical data. Lastly, we kept only the necessary columns that we
  were going to use.

  After all of the data cleaning was done, we saved the new data set
  into a new .csv file.

# Visualization

Provide preliminary visualizations in the form of histograms, density
plots, scatter plots, box-plots, and numerical summaries of the data,
depending on the type of analysis. What do these visualizations suggest
about the hypothesis, model or simulation you are aiming to perform? If
you aim to generate further data visualizations, describe them here.

- By utilizing a simple scatter plot and a regression line, we can see
  that diabetes has a negative relationship with Median Household
  Income, meaning that as income increases diabetes is less prevalent.
  However, seeing that the line is quadratic, we can see minimum
  diabetes levels minimize at around \$108k median income. At every
  income over \$108k, prevalence starts to rise again.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
new_data <- read.csv("cleaned_county_data.csv")
diabetes_data <- new_data %>% 
  filter(MeasureId == "DIABETES")
diabetes_data$Median_Household_Income = as.numeric(diabetes_data$Median_Household_Income)

diabetes_plot = ggplot(diabetes_data, aes(x = Median_Household_Income, y = Data_Value)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), color = "darkred", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "County Median Household Income vs. Diabetes Prevalence",
    subtitle = "CDC PLACES & US Census ACS Data",
    x = "Median Household Income ($)",
    y = "Diabetes Prevalence (%)"
  )
diabetes_plot
```

- We used a similar method to visualize depression percentages.
  Similar to the diabetes graph, it is quadratic. However this graph
  is different as it is a negative quadratic, so as income continues
  to increase, prevalence for depression decreases. Interestingly, at higher incomes,
  the decrease is slighter; the change becomes flatter.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
packages = installed.packages(c("ggplot2"))
library(ggplot2)
depression_plot <- new_data %>% 
  mutate(Median_Household_Income = as.numeric(as.character(Median_Household_Income))) %>%
  filter(MeasureId == "DEPRESSION") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = Median_Household_Income, y = Data_Value)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "darkorchid") + 
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x + I(x^2),
    color = "darkred",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs( 
    title = "Depression Prevalence vs. Median Household Income", 
    subtitle = "CDC PLACES & US Census ACS Data",
    x = "Median Household Income ($)", 
    y = "Depression Prevalence (%)" 
  )

print(depression_plot)

```

# Analysis

Provide some preliminary plans of what analysis you aim to complete.
Mention models, tests, procedures, and some ideas of what expected
outcomes you hope to find

- So far, our project covers the models of 2 diseases in relation to
  household income. Later on, we plan on creating more models, possibly
  around 5 (of all different types– heart conditions, strokes, obesity,
  etc.) We aim to do this in order to get more knowledge on the unknown
  advantages of having higher income. Data will be compared and analyzed
  thoroughly, and we will see if each disease continues to hold a
  negative relationship against median income or if there are some that
  have positive correlation. In the end, we hope to find at least one
  disease that has a positive correlation. We strive to find logical
  reasoning as to why this phenomena takes place– is it simply access
  to better healthcare? is it inability to spend money on better
  food/accomodations? is it a difference in way of life and expectations
  between different income brackets? By comparing data, reading
  literature, and analyzing our results we intend on creating some sort
  of answer.
